findings.evidence: The people operations office publishes the reimbursement log each quarter. [...] The benefits team publishes the reimbursement log after every open enrollment period.
findings.fix: Name one office as the owner of the reimbursement log and state its single publication schedule; if the IT asset group and the benefits team have genuinely distinct responsibilities, say what distinguishes them the first time each is introduced.
findings.location: Program Overview, paragraph 1 and Overview, paragraph 1
findings.violation: Two different named offices, the people operations office and the benefits team, are each stated to be the one that publishes the same reimbursement log, on two different schedules (each quarter versus after every open enrollment period), so the reader cannot tell whether these are the same office under two names, two offices sharing the task, or a genuine contradiction about how often the log appears.

findings.evidence: If the position counts as full-time, the stipend can apply. If the employee has completed 90 days of continuous service, the stipend can apply. If the request arrives before the benefit year ends, the stipend can apply. Only once every condition above is met does the home-office equipment stipend become available to the employee.
findings.fix: State the governing rule first, for example the stipend is available once the position is full-time, the employee has 90 days of continuous service, and the request arrives before the benefit year ends, then list the conditions.
findings.violation: The paragraph opens with three conditional sentences before the fourth sentence finally states the governing rule, so the reader has to hold three unresolved conditions in mind before learning what they add up to.

findings.evidence: The team then routes the request to the correct approver based on department. [...] The finance office reviews every stipend request over 200 dollars before it pays out.
findings.fix: Move the department-routing and dollar-threshold review rules into Approval Timeline, where the reader first learns how a request is reviewed.
findings.location: Program Coordination and Review Responsibility, the document's final content sections
findings.violation: Department-based approver routing and a 200-dollar finance-review threshold are facts a reader needs to predict how long their own request will take, but both arrive only in the document's last two sections, well after Approval Timeline and Required Documentation already described the approval process as though it were complete.

findings.evidence: 36-word sentence, 4 subordinate-clause markers: Then, the review takes longer because the manager who normally handles it is traveling; the backup reviewer who covers for absences was not told that the request needs sign-off before the portal releases the confirmation email.
findings.fix: Split the sentence at a subordinate-clause boundary.
findings.violation: The sentence runs to 36 words with 4 subordinate-clause markers, longer than the reader can hold in mind on a single pass.

findings.evidence: Newest element: the backup reviewer who covers for absences was not told that the request needs sign-off. Full sentence: Then, the review takes longer because the manager who normally handles it is traveling; the backup reviewer who covers for absences was not told that the request needs sign-off before the portal releases the confirmation email.
findings.fix: End the sentence on the process failure, for example: the manager who normally handles this is traveling, and the portal will not release the confirmation email until sign-off happens, so route the request to the backup reviewer, who was never told that sign-off is required.
findings.violation: The sentence's newest and most consequential content, that the backup reviewer was never told sign-off is required, lands in the middle and is followed by a clause about the portal releasing the confirmation email, so the reader's attention lands on the least important part of the sentence instead of the process failure that actually explains the delay.

findings.evidence: The request is reviewed within two business days.
findings.fix: Rewrite the sentence in active voice, naming the actor that performs the action.
findings.violation: The sentence uses a be-verb plus past-participle passive construction in a context where the actor is recoverable and worth naming directly.

findings.evidence: The team logs each request the moment it arrives. The team then routes the request to the correct approver based on department. Once approved, the team schedules the reimbursement for the next pay cycle. The finance office reviews every stipend request over 200 dollars before it pays out.
findings.fix: Either cut the internal-process narration or mark it explicitly as background information for reference, separate from the instructions the employee-reader is meant to follow.
findings.violation: These two sections narrate the benefits and finance teams' own internal workflow in a document otherwise addressed to the employee applying for the stipend, with nothing signaling that the content is background rather than something the reader needs to act on.

findings.evidence: Also, the deposit happens in order to offset costs the employee already paid at this point in time.
findings.fix: Replace the wordy phrase with its plain equivalent (for example, because for due to the fact that).
findings.violation: The sentence uses a wordy construction from the fixed wordy-phrase list that a shorter equivalent would carry with no loss of meaning.

findings.evidence: You record the stipend item on the request form. Finance reconciles the stipend item against the request log each month. Payroll releases the stipend item amount after that monthly review.
findings.fix: Use the same term, such as the request, throughout the document, including in this section, or state explicitly that stipend item is another name for it the first time it appears.
findings.violation: The stipend item is introduced and used three times in this section only, while the rest of the document refers to the same claim as the request, the stipend request, or the reimbursement; nothing signals whether stipend item names the same thing or something new.

findings.evidence: However, reimbursement is not available without a completed receipt.
findings.fix: Restate the sentence with at most one negation, or recast it as a positive statement.
findings.violation: 2 negation markers from the fixed negation list co-occur in one clause, so the reader has to work out the statement's logical sign before understanding it.
